passages.title: Urban trees and summer heat
passages.text:
In a small coastal city, volunteers measured the temperature on two streets at the same hour for ten summer afternoons. One street had mature trees along both sidewalks; the other had almost no shade. The shaded street was cooler on most afternoons, sometimes by several degrees. Residents called the difference proof that planting trees everywhere would solve the city's heat problem.

The volunteers, however, warned against such a broad conclusion. The streets also differed in traffic levels and building heights. Hot exhaust from buses could have affected the measurements, while taller buildings might have blocked sunlight. Because the study compared only two streets, it could not isolate the effect of trees from these other factors.

The volunteers proposed a longer study with sensors placed on several streets. They also suggested measuring temperatures before and after new trees had grown, while recording traffic and nearby construction. Although young trees would not provide immediate shade, such a project could help planners decide where green spaces would be most useful. The first measurements were a promising beginning, not a final answer.

passages.title: The village radio project
passages.text:
When a mountain village lost mobile reception after a storm, a group of students helped the community radio station share important announcements. They collected updates from the local clinic and farmers' cooperative, then read them aloud three times a day. The broadcasts were useful to residents who could not travel easily, particularly older people living far from the village center.

At first, the students assumed that repeating each announcement would be enough. Listeners soon reported that some medical instructions were too fast and that unfamiliar terms caused confusion. The students responded by asking the clinic to approve simpler summaries. They also added a short pause after each instruction so listeners could write it down.

The project did not restore phone service, and the station still needed fuel for its generator. Yet it showed that communication depends on more than sending a message. Information is valuable only if people can understand it and use it. After the mobile network returned, the station kept its slower announcement format because the change had benefited many listeners.

passages.title: Seeds for uncertain seasons
passages.text:
A regional seed library lends small packets of local crop seeds to families. Instead of returning the exact same seeds, borrowers grow the plants and bring back some seeds from their harvest. The library hopes to maintain varieties that have adapted to local conditions and that commercial suppliers may no longer stock.

One family tried a traditional bean during an unusually dry season. The plants survived, but the harvest was smaller than the family expected. A neighbor concluded that the variety was not worth keeping. The library coordinator disagreed: a single difficult season could not show how the bean would perform across different rainfall patterns. She suggested comparing it with other beans over several years.

Keeping a variety is not a promise that it will always produce the largest harvest. It preserves an option that farmers might need when weather changes. The coordinator also reminded borrowers to label seeds carefully; if varieties are mixed or stored while damp, future growers may not receive the seeds they expect. A seed library therefore depends on both patient observation and careful community records.

passages.title: A note in a borrowed book
passages.text:
Every Thursday, Maya returned a borrowed book to the neighborhood reading room. She usually chose books about distant places, although she had rarely traveled beyond her town. One afternoon, she found a pencil note inside a novel: “The ending is not what I expected, but I am glad I continued.” The note had no name or date.

Maya almost erased the writing. The reading room asked visitors not to mark books, and she agreed with that rule. Yet she wondered about the unknown reader who had been surprised enough to leave a message. She copied the sentence onto a scrap of paper and told the librarian, who removed the pencil note carefully.

Weeks later, Maya finished the novel. Its ending was quiet rather than dramatic; a character chose to repair an old friendship instead of leaving home. Maya understood why someone might find it unexpected. She did not know whether she agreed that the ending was satisfying, but she liked the idea that readers could meet a story at different moments and notice different things. She returned the book without adding a note of her own.

choices: Comparing two streets proves all trees cool equally.
Bus pollution is the only cause of urban heat.
Initial observations of shaded streets are encouraging, but further tests are needed.

questions.explanation: Penulis menekankan hasil awal yang menjanjikan dan keterbatasan studi dua jalan.
questions.evidence: The first measurements were a promising beginning, not a final answer.
